---
title: "A1 exercises — Structure, scale and feedback"
---

The questions follow the [tutorial](index.qmd) and [slides](lec.qmd). Answer
each question before opening its answer.

## Levels of organisation

### 1.1

Arrange from the smallest to the largest level: organ, organism, cell,
organ system, tissue.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Cell → tissue → organ → organ system → organism.
:::

### 1.2

In a multicellular animal, most cells exchange materials directly with:

a. the external environment
b. interstitial fluid
c. blood plasma
d. the gut lumen

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b. Interstitial (extracellular) fluid surrounds the cells; blood, where present,
transports material between exchange organs and the tissues.
:::

### 1.3

The intestinal wall contains all four primary tissue types. For each tissue
type, give its main function in the intestine.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| Tissue | Function in the intestine |
| --- | --- |
| Epithelium | Lines the lumen; secretion and absorption |
| Connective tissue | Supports the epithelium and carries blood vessels |
| Smooth muscle | Mixes and moves the contents |
| Nervous tissue | Coordinates secretion and muscle activity |
:::

### 1.4

Put the steps in order for a glucose molecule moving from the gut lumen into
a skeletal-muscle cell:

a. crosses the muscle-cell membrane
b. crosses the apical membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
c. is carried in the blood
d. crosses the basolateral membrane of the intestinal epithelial cell
e. enters the interstitial fluid around the muscle fibre

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

b → d → c → e → a. Glucose in the lumen has not yet been absorbed, because the
lumen is continuous with the outside of the body.
:::

## Surface area, volume and diffusion

### 2.1

Complete the table for cubes with side length $L$.

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | | | |
| 2 | | | |
| 4 | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| $L$ (mm) | Surface area (mm²) | Volume (mm³) | Surface area : volume (mm⁻¹) |
| ---: | ---: | ---: | ---: |
| 1 | 6 | 1 | 6 |
| 2 | 24 | 8 | 3 |
| 4 | 96 | 64 | 1.5 |

The ratio is $6L^2 / L^3 = 6/L$, so each doubling of $L$ halves it.
:::

### 2.2

The time needed for diffusion is proportional to the square of the distance.
By what factor does the diffusion time change when the distance increases
from:

a. 1 µm to 3 µm
b. 0.1 mm to 1 mm
c. 20 µm to 10 µm

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. 3² = 9 times longer.
b. 10² = 100 times longer.
c. (1/2)² = 1/4, i.e. four times shorter.
:::

### 2.3

Name three ways in which large animals overcome the low surface-area-to-volume
ratio of a large body.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

1. Folding, branching or subdivision of exchange surfaces increases the area
   (e.g. alveoli, gill lamellae, intestinal villi).
2. Thin exchange barriers shorten the diffusion distance.
3. Bulk flow (ventilation and circulation) moves material over long distances.
:::

## Tissues

### 3.1

Name the primary tissue type that matches each description.

| | Description |
| --- | --- |
| A | One layer of closely packed cells lining a lumen, with little material between the cells |
| B | Widely spaced cells among abundant parallel extracellular fibres |
| C | Long, cylindrical, striated fibres with many nuclei per fibre |
| D | Cells with long processes, surrounded by many smaller supporting cells |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

A: epithelial tissue (simple epithelium). B: connective tissue (dense regular
connective tissue, e.g. tendon). C: muscle tissue (skeletal muscle).
D: nervous tissue (neurons and glial cells).
:::

### 3.2

Complete the table.

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | | | |
| Cell shape | | | |
| Nuclei per cell | | | |
| Specialised cell junctions | | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Skeletal muscle | Cardiac muscle | Smooth muscle |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Striated? | Yes | Yes | No |
| Cell shape | Long cylindrical fibres | Branched cells | Spindle-shaped cells |
| Nuclei per cell | Many | One (sometimes two) | One |
| Specialised cell junctions | No | Intercalated discs | Gap junctions in many smooth muscles |
:::

### 3.3

Which type of epithelium best suits each function: simple squamous or
stratified squamous?

a. gas exchange
b. protection against abrasion

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Simple squamous: a single thin layer gives a short diffusion distance.
b. Stratified squamous: several cell layers protect the tissue beneath.
:::

### 3.4

Define the terms *lumen*, *apical surface* and *basal surface*.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

- **Lumen:** the inner space of a tube or cavity, such as the gut or a blood vessel.
- **Apical surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the lumen or
  the outside.
- **Basal surface:** the side of an epithelial cell that faces the basement
  membrane and underlying tissue.
:::

### 3.5

A section shows a circular profile with an empty centre. Why is this not
enough to identify it as a blood vessel?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Any tube (such as a duct, gland, gut or vessel) cut in cross-section gives a
ring. An oblique cut through the same tube gives an oval. Identification also
needs the wall structure, its tissue layers and the scale.
:::

## Homeostasis and feedback

### 4.1

Define homeostasis.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Homeostasis is the active maintenance of internal conditions (such as
temperature or the composition of extracellular fluid) within a range
compatible with life, despite external and internal disturbances.
:::

### 4.2

Body temperature in a mammal rises during exercise. Match each item to its
role in the feedback loop: regulated variable, sensor, control centre, effector.

a. sweat glands
b. hypothalamus
c. body temperature
d. thermoreceptors

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. effector; b. control centre; c. regulated variable; d. sensor.
:::

### 4.3

State whether each example is negative or positive feedback.

a. A rise in blood glucose increases insulin secretion, which lowers blood glucose.
b. Uterine contractions increase oxytocin release, which strengthens the contractions.
c. A rise in body temperature increases sweating.
d. Activated clotting factors activate more clotting factors.
e. A fall in blood pressure increases heart rate through the baroreceptor reflex.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Negative. b. Positive. c. Negative. d. Positive. e. Negative.
:::

### 4.4

True or false? Correct any false statements.

a. Positive feedback means that the response is good for the animal.
b. In negative feedback, the response reduces the deviation that triggered it.
c. Positive feedback must have a way to stop.
d. A stable internal concentration means that no transport is taking place.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. False. "Positive" refers to the direction of the loop: the response
   amplifies the original change. It says nothing about benefit.
b. True.
c. True. Otherwise the change keeps growing, as in an action potential or
   during birth.
d. False. Inputs and outputs can balance while transport continues.
:::

## Responses, acclimation and adaptation

### 5.1

Classify each example as an acute response, acclimation or evolutionary
adaptation.

a. Ventilation increases within seconds when an animal starts running.
b. A fish kept at a higher temperature for four weeks changes its enzyme levels.
c. A population of fish living in hypoxic water has inherited larger gill surfaces.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

a. Acute response. b. Acclimation. c. Evolutionary adaptation.
:::

### 5.2

What is the difference between *acclimation* and *acclimatisation*?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

Both are reversible changes within one individual. Acclimation describes the
response to a change in one condition, usually in the laboratory.
Acclimatisation describes the response to changes in the natural environment.
:::

### 5.3

Complete the table comparing oxygen delivery to the tissues.

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | | |
| Exchange surface | | |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | | |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | | |

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Answer

| | Insect | Mammal |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Respiratory medium | Air | Air |
| Exchange surface | Tracheoles, the fine endings of the tracheae, at the tissues | Alveoli in the lungs |
| Route from exchange surface to the tissue cells | Air-filled tracheae branch directly to the tissues | Blood carries O₂, mostly bound to haemoglobin, from lungs to tissues |
| Role of the circulatory system in O₂ transport | Small | Essential |
:::
